standfirst: An interpreter whose entire professional ethic is invisibility gets assigned to a star whose public voice he has been quietly rewriting, and every press conference turns into a test of what he is willing to say on her behalf. The pull is the gap between what she means, what he translates, and what neither of them says. The picks below are built around that gap: professional intimacy, watching somebody be edited, and two people who can only be honest inside a job.

picks.why: The closest thing to it in tone and in subject. Two people whose work is other people's stories, circling each other for years while neither says the direct thing. Same interest in language as a hiding place, same beautifully shot restraint, same second story about an older couple that quietly outclasses the main one. Difference: it is much sadder and much slower, and the grief underneath it never gets resolved the way a romcom resolves things.

For the specific discomfort of being observed while you are trying to be a person. A camera crew instead of an interpreter, two people whose worst version of themselves is on film, and a script that understands how much of a relationship is performance management. Difference: the leads have a shared past and the show trades on nostalgia rather than on the thrill of a first meeting.

The other 2025 romance about competence as attraction. A headhunter and the man whose life she keeps organising, both of them adults, no manufactured misunderstandings, and a workplace where the job is real rather than a backdrop. Difference: it is warm and safe the whole way through. There is no cruelty in either lead and no reveal to be afraid of.

Professional invisibility as a romance engine. Somebody very good at making other people look good, a workplace where words are the product, and a slow admission that the arrangement has stopped being professional. Difference: the power sits with the man and the show is far gentler about it, so none of the loyalty tests that drive Can This Love Be Translated exist here.

If the appeal was the power imbalance: a very famous woman, a man who works for her family, and a marriage that runs on managed statements. Same pleasure in watching a hard woman drop the public register for exactly one person. Difference: it is a melodrama with a terminal diagnosis at its centre, so it plays for devastation where this plays for flutter.

The pure form of the service relationship romance: nine years of anticipating a difficult person's needs, then one resignation letter. Same dynamic where the job is intimacy in disguise. Difference: it is a broad comedy with no interest in the ethics of the arrangement, and the childhood trauma plot is decoration rather than the point.

against.title: Business Proposal
against.why: The default romcom pick, handed out for any Korean romance with a workplace and an office secret. It is a cartoon, deliberately and successfully, with no interior life for anybody. What makes Can This Love Be Translated work is the quiet: a man deciding, live, which version of a sentence to give the room. Nothing in Business Proposal is quiet.

against.title: Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha
against.why: Paired for the lead, which is the only connection. That one is a healing drama about a village absorbing a stranger, and its whole register is comfort. This is a show about performance and editing, set in hotel corridors and interview rooms in two countries. Watch both, in whichever order, but not expecting the same thing twice.

against.title: Something in the Rain
against.why: Suggested for the age gap and the workplace, and it will disappoint anyone who came for the wordplay. That show is about an office turning on a woman for a private choice, filmed with long silences and very little pleasure. The interpreting premise here generates jokes and tension in the same scene. Different appetite entirely.
